_: English prose for the story line. Same shape as story.json minus the `skills` fingerprint: the translation covers prose only and maps to missions by position, exactly like pack translations. Em dashes are counted by test:prose-en; the budget for this file is 0.

sql.opening:
You have started as an analyst at a distributor of FMCG and over-the-counter pharma. The company moves goods from manufacturers into chains, pharmacies, traditional retail and online; two and a half years of data sit in the database you have just been given access to.

Nine missions cover your first weeks: from "pull me the price list" to "work out why the brand collapsed". The people asking are the same ones you meet outside the line: the brand manager, finance, the commercial director.
sql.ending:
The base is covered. You have gone from a plain selection to a full business case, and you know where SQL stays silent: a join that multiplies rows, a NULL that eats your filter, a grain nobody mentioned.

The other half of the track is still there, and it is the practice. A session picks what is due for review from it, and adds what the line never touched.

missions.title: First day
missions.hook: The first thing you are asked for is not a report but an extract: the brand manager needs the price list, finance needs part of it. Every piece of work against a database starts with the same two questions: which columns, and which rows.
missions.outcome: You pull the columns you need out of a table and cut the rows you do not. Every later query in the track starts here.

missions.title: Top of the list, empty cells
missions.hook: People rarely want the whole list. They want the top: the ten most expensive items, the worst outlets of the month. Along the way you discover a third state besides yes and no, and that an ordinary filter says nothing about it.
missions.outcome: You take a top-N by any measure and stop losing rows to empty values. That loss is the most common silent one in reporting.

missions.title: From rows to numbers
missions.hook: The first question an extract cannot answer: how much did we sell in March. An extract returns forty thousand rows; the answer is one number. And the raw layer turns out to lie: duplicates, dates in four formats, one chain spelled two ways.
missions.outcome: You collapse rows into numbers at the grain you were asked for, and you check raw data before a report is built on it.

missions.title: Lookups
missions.hook: The sales table holds identifiers, while your manager asks about brands, cities and channels. The names live elsewhere and have to be attached. You also find out that filtering before the count and filtering after it are two different answers.
missions.outcome: You join facts to lookup tables, and you tell a filter on rows apart from a filter on groups that are already counted.

missions.title: Zero and absence
missions.hook: You are asked for a report across all outlets, including the ones that bought nothing this month. A plain join drops them without a word, and the report looks better than reality. The same request needs slices: promo and non-promo side by side, not one total.
missions.outcome: You show absence as absence rather than as a vanished row, and you count several slices in a single pass.

missions.title: When the number doubles
missions.hook: You add one more table to the query and revenue doubles. No error, no warning: the join multiplied the rows. This is exactly the class of mistake the track introduction was written for. The query ran; the answer is wrong.
missions.outcome: You catch row multiplication before the number reaches the person who asked, and you break a heavy query into steps that read on their own.

missions.title: What to compare against
missions.hook: A number on its own means nothing: is 2088 units a week a lot or a little? Meaning appears next to a reference point, and an analyst has three of them: the weeks before a promotion, the previous period, and the neighbours in the same group. Choosing between them is the job.
missions.outcome: You measure uplift against a base you name out loud, rankings inside groups, and comparisons with the previous period.

missions.title: The promise and the fact
missions.hook: Two topics about the same thing from different sides. The company promised something, a price list at the start of the month, a demand forecast three months before it, and then looked at what actually happened. In both cases the gap is not one person making a mistake. It is a quantity you have to measure and then explain.
missions.outcome: You work out how much of the list price reached the till and what ate the rest, and you measure forecast error so that misses cannot cancel each other out, with a free benchmark standing next to it.

missions.title: Why it dropped
missions.hook: The last question arrives as worry rather than a task: a brand has halved and nobody knows why. There is no new technique here, only every earlier one in the right order. Deciding which query to write is worth more than being able to write it.
missions.outcome: You take a situation apart down to its cause, the numbers first and then what they mean for the business, and you say out loud what the data cannot know.

python.opening:
Same company, same dataset, a different tool. A query hands you a finished answer; in pandas the data stays in your hands as an object you keep working on: reshape it, smooth a series, join it with a file that was never in the database.

Five missions cover what an analyst does in a notebook, from "I read the table and I know what is in it" to "the same calculation, without a loop over rows". The track is written as a continuation of SQL and explains some of its ideas by comparison, which blocks nothing here.
python.ending:
The base is covered. You have gone from "what is in the variable" to a chain that computes a whole column at once, and you know where pandas stays silent: an index that took the column, a missing value in a grouping key, a join that multiplied rows, a copy standing in for the original data.

The finale here is not a business case but a habit of writing so that the calculation survives the next question. The other half of the track is still there, and it is the practice. A session picks what is due for review from it, and adds what the line never touched.

missions.title: What is in the variable
missions.hook: In a database the column types are declared and the engine picks the order of evaluation. Here it is the other way round: steps run exactly as written, and nobody declared the types, they were guessed while reading. So the first thing you learn is not a calculation but the habit of knowing, after every line, what is now in the variable: a table or a column, a number or text.
missions.outcome: You select rows with a mask and columns through loc, and you look at the types before the arithmetic rather than after a sum of numbers has glued strings together.

missions.title: The index and the first summary
missions.hook: The first summary brings a question SQL never asks: the column you grouped by has disappeared from the table. It has not disappeared. It moved into the index, a structure kept apart from the data that decides how rows line up with each other. And before any summary it is worth looking at the data itself: one stray category moves an average further than you would expect.
missions.outcome: You build a summary with groupby knowing in advance what comes back and what ends up in the index, and you catch an outlier or a stray category before either reaches the report.

missions.title: A summary that comes back to the rows
missions.hook: A summary rarely just gets shown. More often its value has to come back to every row: the share of this sale in the sales of that product, a rank inside a brand. That is what transform is for. Two silent losses surface in the same place: grouping drops rows with a missing key without a word, and a join on a key that is not unique multiplies them just as quietly.
missions.outcome: You return a value at the original grain, you stop losing rows to a missing key, and you check the cardinality of a join before the total grows several times over.

missions.title: The shape of the table
missions.hook: Next the data has to be moved rather than counted. The receiving system takes the long format only, a human wants the same report wide, and a shipment series has to be monthly although the database keeps it weekly. Shape here is not decoration: it decides how many steps the next calculation will take.
missions.outcome: You move a table between wide and long, change the frequency of a series with resample, compute a rolling window, and bring the data to a state where one row is one observation.

missions.title: The chain and the cost of a step
missions.hook: The last mission is not about a new calculation but about how it is written. A flag set on a slice never reaches the original table, and the code does not complain once. And apply over rows gives the same answer as a vectorised operation: on a table of regions you cannot see the difference, on the sales table it is the difference between a second and a minute.
missions.outcome: You write transformations as a chain and you know where a copy appears and where a view on the original data does, and you replace a loop over rows with a vectorised operation, because the difference here is an order of magnitude rather than a matter of style.
